title: Five of Wands: Give Different Efforts Shared Rules

quickTake.upright: Everyone is making an effort; first establish what the disagreement is about
quickTake.reversed: Disagreement may be avoided, or the argument may be growing more chaotic

introMarkdown:
Upright in one sentence: Everyone is making an effort; first establish what the disagreement is about.

Reversed in one sentence: Disagreement may be avoided, or the argument may be growing more chaotic.

Five people each hold a staff and make expansive movements, yet their common direction is unclear. The Five of Wands’ most useful question is not “Who will win?” but “Are these efforts trying to do the same thing?”

sections.title: Five people exert themselves without a shared direction
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Beneath a blue sky, five people in short tunics of different colors and patterns stand on uneven ground. One raises a staff upright, another above the shoulder, and another angles it toward the center. Five long staffs cross in the air. The foreground figure has their back to us, and the others’ bodies and gazes are not fully aligned in one direction.

There is no blood and no clear leader occupying the center. The crossed staffs might suggest an argument, but could also resemble training or a game. The image alone cannot establish everyone’s intentions, and not every disagreement can be read as hostility. Different clothes are visible facts; different goals are an interpretation requiring verification.

The crossing staffs crowd the picture, yet each person’s position remains distinguishable on the ground. That contrast is useful: opinions can collide while participants still need to know where they stand and where they can step back. A lack of shared direction does not mean disagreement must be eliminated. Sometimes stating each person’s purpose turns confusion into an exercise that can be designed. But where actual intimidation or harm exists, Waite’s mention of mock combat cannot be used to minimize it as normal adjustment.

sections.title: Understanding competition through mock combat
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Waite describes a group who may be engaged in sport or strife and explicitly refers to mock combat. He also connects the card with competition and efforts to achieve results. Its historical themes therefore extend beyond interpersonal arguments to practice and striving to get ahead.

The old book’s reversed entry mentions disputes, litigation, and contradiction. This article retains the need to address differences without predicting legal disputes. The discussion rules, collaborative adjustment, and conflict avoidance below are original modern learning applications.

sections.title: Understanding the upright card
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Upright, the card can reveal a situation that is not yet coordinated. One person values speed, another quality, and another wants their proposal to be noticed. If people are addressing different levels of the issue, greater investment can lead to more collisions. Clarify goals, resources, and evaluation criteria separately so differences have a chance to yield useful information.

Competition with rules can also support practice. You can compare methods, test views, and hear objections without turning winning or losing into a measure of someone’s worth. Participants must know the rules, be able to disagree, and leave the discussion with a clear next step.

sections.title: Understanding the reversed card
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Here, reversal offers two things to check: has conflict been pushed out of view, or has it become draining with no way forward? If no one openly objects but everyone acts on a different understanding, the problem remains. Repeatedly arguing over the same phrase does not necessarily mean proposals are being seriously compared.

Narrow the issue temporarily, address one observable difference, and agree what information will decide it. If specific threats or disrespect occur, respond to the actual behavior and seek appropriate support. “Necessary adjustment” is no reason to require yourself to keep enduring it.

Both upright and reversed readings may involve arguments; loudness need not distinguish them. More useful is whether disagreement produces new information: what was learned, who can decide, and whether the rules are mutually acceptable. Upright in an obstacle position may indicate competition crowding out cooperation. Reversed in an advice position may invite letting go of unnecessary winning, rather than always giving way.

sections.title: Band rehearsal does not require everyone to win
sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Original fictional case.** A five-person amateur band is preparing a community performance. The guitarist wants an extra solo, the singer worries the song is too long, and the drummer wants a faster tempo. Everyone prepares seriously, but every discussion becomes a popularity vote. Their question is: “How can we stop arguing about arrangements at every rehearsal?” They draw the Five of Wands upright in the current-cooperation position.

Five staffs reach into the center at once, like several worthwhile ideas competing for the same stretch of time. The absence of an obvious conductor suggests asking about decision rules before identifying a “difficult person.” Waite’s mock combat offers another angle: turn the argument into short trial performances so different methods face the same goal. Enthusiasm can become useful material if everyone knows what they are trying to resolve.

If the real disagreement is that someone cannot accept the repertoire, trial performances cannot replace a discussion about willingness to participate. If budget or equipment rules out an arrangement, eliminate infeasible options first. Objections sometimes identify necessary limits rather than obstruct creativity.

They first agree on the performance length, then play both versions once, recording them to compare only transitions and how they sound. A person agreed in advance will finalize the submitted version. Other ideas remain for a later rehearsal, giving disagreement an outlet without turning it into judgments about character.

sections.title: Why does everyone work separately when no one objects?
sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Original fictional case.** Friends take turns hosting a book club. They seldom argue openly, but people have canceled at the last minute on three occasions. Some want serious discussion of the text, while others want relaxed conversation. The host avoids asking because they fear disturbing the peace. The question is: “How should the book club handle everyone saying they don’t mind?” They draw the Five of Wands reversed in the hidden-obstacle position.

Imagining the crossed staffs as different, unstated purposes suggests a modern reversed reading: conflict may not have disappeared, but lost the chance for open coordination. The known differences in goals support this approach, while last-minute absences alone do not prove disrespect. The reading focuses on making needs speakable rather than generating new accusations.

It is also possible that everyone shares a goal but recent dates simply do not work. If inquiry reveals specific scheduling conflicts behind the absences, change the date. If someone clearly wants to leave, demanding further participation has no point. “Not joining this round” needs to be an accepted option.

Before the next meeting, the host asks what everyone hopes to get from the hour and proposes a trial: textual discussion in the first half, free conversation in the second. They will gather feedback after two meetings. People who dislike the format can skip it rather than communicate disagreement through silence.

sections.title: A small exercise
sections.bodyMarkdown: Recall a disagreement. Write down each side’s proposed solution and the need behind it. Then write a sentence to check your understanding: “Are we trying to solve… and… respectively?” Test understanding only; do not yet require agreement.

sections.title: Common misreadings
sections.bodyMarkdown: The Five of Wands does not automatically mean someone is targeting you, nor does it guarantee that every argument is healthy competition. Check actual behavior and rules before deciding whether this is useful adjustment, differing goals, or a draining process that should stop.
